title: What 264 Hours Without Sleep Does to Your Brain

strategy.viewer: Curious adults who have pulled an all-nighter and wonder how bad it really gets; clicks for the extreme record and the 'drunk brain' hook.
strategy.hook: Seventeen hours awake is like being drunk; eleven days and your brain starts sleeping while you are awake: a familiar fact against an impossible one.
strategy.promise: What really happens in your brain from hour 0 to hour 264 without sleep, with the real cases (Tripp, Gardner) and the science.
strategy.payoff: A brain that will not sleep starts sleeping in pieces (local sleep, microsleeps) while awake, and without full sleep its cleaning flow (glymphatic) never completes.
strategy.takeaway: Stay awake long enough and your brain starts sleeping without you.

scenes.text: Stay awake seventeen hours, and your brain performs like you are drunk.
We will follow one brain, hour by hour, past the point where it begs to shut down.
label: HOUR 0
You wake up

scenes.text: Hour zero: adenosine starts building sleep pressure. At seventeen hours awake, you perform like a blood alcohol of point zero five. At twenty-four, point one.
Around hour twenty, reaction times slow and mistakes pile up.
Caffeine does not erase that pressure. It only blocks the receptors that sense it.
That is why drowsy driving kills. Not hours of sleep at the wheel, just seconds, with nobody noticing.
label: HOUR 20+
Slower, edgier, forgetful

scenes.text: Hour thirty. Eyes open, answering questions. But parts of your brain may already be asleep.
In 2011, researchers recorded rats kept awake. Patches of cortex switched off, like sleep, while the animal stayed on its feet.
scenes.code:
title=Text("LOCAL SLEEP",font_size=46,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
cells=VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.7,color=GREY_B,fill_color=ORANGE,fill_opacity=0.9,stroke_width=2).move_to(RIGHT*(i-3.5)*0.8+UP*(1.2-j*0.8)) for j in range(3) for i in range(8)])
sub=Text("an awake brain, tired in patches",font_size=32,color=WHITE).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(cells),run_time=1.5)
self.play(FadeIn(sub),run_time=0.8)
import random
random.seed(4)
for _ in range(4):
    pick=random.sample(range(24),5)
    self.play(*[cells[i].animate.set_fill(GREY_E,opacity=1) for i in pick],run_time=0.7)
    self.wait(0.4)
    self.play(*[cells[i].animate.set_fill(ORANGE,opacity=0.9) for i in pick],run_time=0.5)

scenes.caption: DRIVEN BLIND IN A 10-SECOND MICROSLEEP AT 100 KM/H
scenes.text: Ten seconds of microsleep at a hundred kilometers an hour: almost three hundred meters, driven blind.
Night-shift workers and exhausted office staff can end up in this zone. Sleep scientists treat it as a public safety issue.
label: WHO LIVES HERE
Nights, long calls, long roads

scenes.text: Hour thirty-six. Mood sags, and the brain's alarm center, the amygdala, reacts far more strongly to bad news.
label: HOUR 36
Emotions get louder
scenes.fact: Yoo et al. 2007: amygdala response ~60%\Nstronger after a night without sleep.

scenes.text: Memory takes a hit too. After one night without sleep, a study found about nineteen percent fewer new memories retained.
Hour forty-eight. Attention lapses grow longer and more frequent.
Hour seventy-two. Concentration crumbles, speech slows, and the world starts to blur.
label: HOUR 72
The edge of reality

scenes.text: 1959: disc jockey Peter Tripp stays awake two hundred one hours. By day three, he reportedly sees spiders in his shoes. By day five, a doctor is an undertaker.
scenes.fact: Accounts of Tripp vary; hallucinations\Nand paranoia are well documented.

scenes.heading: RANDY GARDNER, 1963
scenes.text: San Diego, four years later. Seventeen-year-old Randy Gardner sets out to beat the record for a school science project. Eleven days.
On day four he reportedly mistakes a street sign for a person. On the last night, he beats sleep researcher William Dement at pinball.
label: DAY 4 TO DAY 11
Confused, yet still capable
scenes.fact: Dement's 1964 observations of Gardner:\Nlapses, yet flashes of normal function.

scenes.text: After 264 hours, Gardner sleeps about fourteen hours, then is largely back to normal within days.
Please do not try this. He was young, healthy and watched around the clock, and still showed slurred speech, paranoia and memory lapses.
Your brain has no lymph vessels. So at night, fluid flushes it instead: in 2013, sleeping mice showed the space between cells growing about sixty percent, and waste washing out faster.
scenes.code:
title=Text("THE GLYMPHATIC FLUSH",font_size=44,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
def cells(gap,col):
    return VGroup(*[Circle(radius=0.55,color=col,fill_color=col,fill_opacity=0.5).move_to(RIGHT*(i-1.5)*(1.1+gap)+UP*(j-0.5)*(1.1+gap)) for i in range(4) for j in range(2)]).shift(DOWN*0.4)
a=cells(0.0,RED_C)
lab=Text("AWAKE: tight spaces, waste lingers",font_size=34,color=RED_C).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(a),FadeIn(lab),run_time=1.5)
dots=VGroup(*[Dot(RIGHT*(i-2.5)*0.9+UP*(j-0.5)*0.3+DOWN*0.4,color=YELLOW,radius=0.07) for i in range(6) for j in range(2)])
self.play(FadeIn(dots),run_time=0.8)
b=cells(0.55,BLUE_C)
lab2=Text("ASLEEP: spaces ~60% wider, waste flushed",font_size=34,color=BLUE_C).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(Transform(a,b),Transform(lab,lab2),dots.animate.shift(RIGHT*6.5),run_time=3.5)

scenes.text: That waste includes beta-amyloid, linked to Alzheimer's. One 2018 study found a single sleepless night raised it about five percent in some regions. That does not prove one night causes dementia.
The fix is boring and powerful: seven to nine hours, regular timing, and a short nap can reset the worst microsleeps for a while.
So what happens to a brain that will not sleep? It does not stop. It starts sleeping in pieces while you are awake, and its night-time clean-up gets cut short.
If this changed how you see tonight, subscribe for the next one. And tell me in the comments: what is the longest you have ever stayed awake?
Seventeen hours without sleep makes you perform about like a driver at point zero five.
Study after study found the same thing: your attention slides with every hour awake.
At twenty-four hours, it is about point one, over the legal limit in many countries.
And caffeine does not fix it. It only hides the signal.
The full story is on the channel. Subscribe for the next one.
In 1963, a seventeen-year-old in San Diego stayed awake for two hundred sixty-four hours, for a school science project.
By the end he had slurred speech, memory lapses and paranoia, and doctors wired him to an EEG.
Then he slept about fourteen hours, and recovered.
The full story is on the channel. Subscribe for the next one.

shorts.title: Your brain cleans itself at night

scenes.text: Your brain has no lymph vessels, yet it washes itself every night.
In sleeping mice, the space between brain cells grows by about sixty percent.
Waste, including amyloid, gets flushed out faster. In one study, a sleepless night raised amyloid by about five percent.
The full story is on the channel. Subscribe for the next one.

titles: What 264 Hours Without Sleep Does to Your Brain
Your Brain After 11 Days Without Sleep
Why Your Brain Starts Sleeping While Awake

youtube.description:
What happens to your brain after 24, 48, 72 hours without sleep, and beyond? From the drunk-like brain to microsleeps, hallucinations, and the clean-up your brain does at night, with the real cases of Peter Tripp (1959) and Randy Gardner (1963).

In this video:
- Awake too long
- The drunk brain
- Seeing things
- The night shift

FAQ
How long can a person stay awake? The best-known documented experiment is 264 hours (Gardner, 1963-64); it is dangerous and not recommended.
What is a microsleep? A lapse of a fraction of a second up to about 30 s when the brain briefly sleeps.
Does sleep clean the brain? In mice, the space between cells widens ~60% in sleep and waste clears faster (Xie 2013).

Tell me in the comments: what is your longest time awake?

Sources: Dawson & Reid 1997, Nature 388; Williamson & Feyer 2000, Occup Environ Med; Vyazovskiy et al. 2011, Nature 472; Nir et al. 2017, Nature Medicine 23; Yoo et al. 2007, Current Biology (amygdala) and Nature Neuroscience (memory); Xie et al. 2013, Science 342; Shokri-Kojori et al. 2018, PNAS 115; Gulevich, Dement & Johnson 1966, Arch Gen Psychiatry (Gardner).
